globalRules: Every opinion is attributed to a named fictional discipline/report/version and materials considered.
Analytical results, observations, interpretations, factual causation and legal causation remain separate.
An expert does not determine actor identity, intent, guilt, witness credibility or the ultimate legal issue.
A joint statement is authoritative for the agreements and disagreements it records at its date; it does not become a judicial finding or rewrite scientific truth.

The latest individual report or addendum governs that expert's individual position where the point is not superseded or covered by the joint statement; earlier reports remain visible for opinion changes.
Service does not prove admissibility. Any judicial ruling governs permitted use, not the underlying scientific observation or opinion.
Prosecution and defence expert disclosure/service/privilege states are explicit.
No numerical probability or categorical conclusion is invented beyond the fictional expert source.

designedLimitations: more than one blunt-impact mechanism medically plausible
injury pattern does not uniquely identify object
limited ability to time injury within a narrow incident window
clinical treatment and susceptibility require contextual analysis
overlap between direct blow and fall patterns
timing range rather than exact timestamp
sampling occurred after incident and treatment
medication adherence/timing not proved by one result
post-event clinical administration must be excluded from interpretation where relevant

mustNotBeUsedAloneFor: categorical source attribution where mixture does not support it
designedLimitations: damaged edge is not proof of impact
derived timeline has no authority beyond cited sources
absence of note is not proof event did not occur

specialistReviewRequired: Home Office registered forensic pathologist or appropriately qualified homicide-pathology reviewer for realism/limits
appropriately qualified toxicology reviewer for analytical and interpretive design
criminal practitioner for admissibility, expert directions, service, disclosure and legal-causation boundaries
forensic-quality reviewer against the then-current Forensic Science Regulator Code and CrimPR Part 19
